item.title: 🪞 Why does the brain keep selling you a new "me"?
item.description:
Your “me” is a live build

Heather Berlin, Ethan Kross, and Nicole Vignola (Big Think) argue that a stable “me” is a live mix. Perception mixes internal expectations (what past experience taught you to expect) with external sensory input (what your senses pick up now). Because that mix runs in real time, thoughts, attention, and the story you tell about yourself can change what you feel as “me” tomorrow.

You pull the evidence your mood already wants

Prior experience wires the mind. The brain strengthens the connections that matter and lets others wither (neural pruning). Mood then decides what you notice, and later recall, even when the kitchen has not changed. In a negative headspace you pull more negative evidence; in a positive headspace you pull more positive evidence.

item.title: 🧠🔮 Your brain is a controlled hallucination
item.description:
Denoising reality

Instead of waiting for data, your brain runs a continuous prediction loop. It generates a best-guess model of the world and uses sensory input to correct errors.

What if everything you are seeing, hearing, and feeling is not actually reality? It is a controlled hallucination your brain constructs.

Sensory neurons “poke” the brain, which immediately generates a model to explain the disturbance. It then checks how that prediction matches incoming data, using past experience (priors) to denoise reality until the model and the senses align.
